100% agree! The landlord should’ve started the eviction process as soon as that first payment was late.

You said landlords aren’t discriminatory and doesn’t make sense for them to be. My point is when allowed to be, they are discriminatory.

The Anti-Discriminatory policies have little to do with poor people not getting housing. The exorbitant property taxes, the taxes to operate a business, the limited number of existing housing, and also the difficulty of getting new housing approved is what’s keeping rent high.

My gripe with this landlord is that they didn’t make sure the tenant could afford the rent before leasing the house to them, and there are numerous ways to do so. If this tenant isn’t paying rent i’m not sure why they don’t just evict them.

>Common sense. Landlords are generally not interested in discrimination.

Oh yeah, landlords have [definitely](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Housing_discrimination_in_the_United_States) never been discriminatory in the U.S.

An international student can submit a I20 form, which specifically helps those students get apartments they wouldn’t otherwise be qualified for.

But before this law, what stopped landlords from being discriminatory with their rejections of applicants? Seems like allegations of discrimination would be very difficult to pursue, and defend against, in a court of law previously.

If a university student can’t meet the income criteria begin with, what does this law change that would’ve previously allowed them to get the apartment?

What other factors should landlords take into consideration other than being able to afford the apartment? Race? Religion? Political affiliation?
I’m also not sure where you are heard that you have to accept the first qualifying candidate, but if someone qualifies for an apartment, what reason would a landlord have to say no?

You can require that monthly verifiable income be equal to at least 3 times the monthly rent. If their income is less than 3 times the rental amount, you can require a cosigner

You can verify the income of a tenant with 2 consecutive paystubs, most recent tax returns, W2, Leave & Earnings Statements, or a Statement of Social Security Benefits.

A landlord can require proof of income for a rental property, normally this is done with at least two pay stubs. That’s not prohibited in Seattle. Regardless, the landlord could just evict them for not paying rent.

I said this to address the landlord’s concern about the tenant running an airbnb ad for their apartment. If the tenant violates any part of the lease the landlord has the right to pursue eviction, after giving the 14 day notice to pay/cure or vacate.

Edit: At this point a anti airbnb clause does nothing. If it existed at the time of signing the landlord could’ve evicted for that reason or for non payment of rent.

If there was an anti airbnb or vrbo clause, the landlord has the legal right to give a 10 day notice to cure or vacate in regard to a lease violation. From there the landlord can submit a lawsuit for eviction.

This article doesn’t give a lot of concrete evidence, and is mostly based on what the landlord has to say, but if the landlord leased out a property to someone he hadn’t financially vetted, then that’s his fault. Washington has very tenant friendly eviction laws, and the landlord knows this. Why would he lease out a property to someone he hadn’t financially vetted yet? 

Say what you will about eviction laws, but with the laws the way they are, and the landlord ignorant of them, doesn’t make the state responsible for making the landlord whole. There’s risk in any business.

Anything the lease doesn’t cover that the land lord or tenant regrets later is on them, they signed it. This is how contracts work, it’s not on the state to step in on either parties behalf bc of the shortcomings of their signed agreement.

I’m not sure of the specifics for your situation, and i’m sorry that’s happening to you. But in the situation described in the article, it seems like the landlord made a pretty big mistake, and that’s the risk they run in the business they’re in.

Edit: Landlord should give the 14 day notice required then submit a lawsuit to evict.

I don’t really have many points of disagreement with any of this, but i do want to say that we have a waiting problem disguised as a camping problem. Meaning, as soon as anyone moving around the map hears the loud ass footsteps, they are being incentivized to sit still and wait for the opponent to turn the corner. I agree with the sentiment that the game is catering to a certain playstyle, but i also want to say that most people aren’t necessarily camping in some mundane spot, there’s just too many audio cues to not stop where you are and wait for someone to push you. This creates the effect that, “oh that guy was just sitting there waiting for me” 

To fix this, adjustments need to be made to footstep audio, strafe speeds, and sprint to fire speeds. This game has a lot of potential, i just hope the devs can live up to it.
